analysis.one_liner: Bans defense contractors who caused serious injury or death or committed fraud from getting Pentagon contracts for five years.
analysis.headline: The bill to debar negligent or fraudulent defense contractors was referred to the House Armed Services Committee and died there without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Secretary of Defense to bar companies from Defense Department contracts for at least five years if they caused serious injury or death to government personnel through gross negligence or recklessness, or committed contract fraud. It would also bar subcontractors found at fault, penalize prime contractors for bad subcontractors, and strip award and incentive fees from contractors hit with the most serious corrective action requests. The only exception is a national security waiver decided by the Secretary himself.
analysis.who_benefits: Soldiers, civilian defense personnel, and taxpayers. Anyone whose safety depends on contractors performing defense work would gain a government that stops doing business with companies found to have killed or injured people through gross negligence, and fraud-related contracting costs would be put under a mandatory penalty instead of a discretionary slap on the wrist.

how_it_helps.text: Mandates at least a five-year debarment of any contractor found, in a criminal, civil, or administrative proceeding, to have caused serious injury or death to government personnel through gross negligence or reckless disregard for safety, or to have committed fraud [S3].
Extends the ban to subcontractors found at fault and forbids prime contractors from using them, closing the common practice of shifting work to subsidiaries after a violation [S3].

Requires the Secretary to withhold all award and incentive fees from a contractor that receives a level III corrective action request from the Defense Contract Management Agency, and claw back fees already paid that year [S3].
Covers contracts over $500,000, reaching the bulk of defense procurement, and lets the Secretary waive a debarment only on a case-by-case finding that it would jeopardize national security [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors found negligent or fraudulent: they would lose Pentagon business for at least five years in the same line of goods or services, forfeit award and incentive fees, and lose the leeway to keep contracts through settlements with no admission of fault.

drawbacks.text: The debarment applies only to contracts for the same or similar goods or services as the contract where the violation occurred, so a violator could keep selling other products to the Pentagon [S3].

The Secretary of Defense could waive any debarment on a case-by-case national security finding, which critics of the existing debarment system say is how mandatory penalties become optional in practice [S3].

Because liability can be triggered by civil settlements and administrative findings with consent or compromise, some contractors argue mandatory debarment would push companies to settle cases abroad or litigate rather than fix problems quickly; critics of mandatory debarment also note it can reduce competition and raise contract prices in the short run [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct: people killed or injured by grossly negligent contractors currently sit in a system where companies routinely keep their contracts, and this would make a five-year ban automatic. The bill is modest in scope — it applies only to similar work, and the Secretary keeps a national security escape hatch — so the main cost is some rigidity and possible short-term price increases where a debarred company is hard to replace. On balance, the burden falls on companies already found at fault, not on the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Armed Services Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died at the end of the 111th Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Carol Shea-Porter introduced the Safety in Defense Contracting Act on June 11, 2009 with eight fellow Democrats [S1] [S5].
Nine House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services the day it was introduced and appears in the record only at that referral; no further committee or floor action is listed before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors that have caused injuries or deaths through negligence or committed procurement fraud are better off: the mandatory five-year ban and fee forfeiture never became law, so the existing discretionary debarment system — under which companies frequently keep their contracts — remained in place.

for.name: Carol Shea-Porter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring mandatory debarment of negligent or fraudulent defense contractors and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor [S1] [S5].

for.name: 9 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Gwen Moore, Russ Carnahan, Jim McGovern, Jan Schakowsky, Peter DeFazio, Glenn Nye, and Tim Bishop [S3] [S4].

against.name: House Committee on Armed Services
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up after referral; it received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat (9 of 253 House Democrats), but no votes were ever taken and no Republican is on record for or against the bill, so the partisan split cannot be measured.

industries.note: Companies found to have caused serious injury or death through gross negligence, or to have committed fraud, would lose Pentagon contracts for at least five years and forfeit award and incentive fees after the most serious corrective action requests. Their gain from the bill failing is keeping a system in which responsibility for injuring government personnel rarely costs them the contract.

industries.industry: Military and civilian defense personnel and taxpayers
industries.note: The bill's beneficiaries would have been the troops and government employees whose safety depends on contractor performance, and taxpayers who pay for fraud. The bill's failure left their protection where it was.
